project.name: Q3 Release Train — Version Integrity Sweep
project.description: Five services cut releases this train. Before the combined release notes go out, you need to check each one: does the tag's version bump actually match what the commit itself claims to be - a fix, a feature, or a breaking change? Not by trusting how orderly the tag sequence looks, but by reading what each commit actually says against the bump its tag carries.
project.ticket: Q3 Release Train — Version Integrity Sign-off

start.speaker: Narrator
start.narrative: Five services, five releases, one release train closing out. You decide to check each one before the combined release notes go out - one at a time, comparing each commit's own conventional-commit type against the version bump its tag actually carries.

check-nova-auth.speaker: You
check-nova-auth.narrative: Release 1 of 5: Nova Auth. The previous release, v1.0.1, was a plain fix. The new commit on top of it is tagged v1.0.2 - one more patch in the sequence.

a2.message: feat!: replace session cookies with JWT, breaking all existing sessions

check-nova-auth.prompt: Does v1.0.2's tag match what its own commit says it is?

choices.label: No - the commit starts with "feat!:", a breaking change, tagged as a mere patch
Yes - it's the next patch in an otherwise ordinary sequence

auth-pushback.speaker: Renata
auth-pushback.narrative: "Ordinary sequence, sure - but did you actually read v1.0.2's own commit message, or just look at how the version numbers line up?"

auth-escalate.speaker: You
auth-escalate.narrative: You judged the tag by how orderly the sequence looked, not by what the commit it points to actually says.
auth-escalate.prompt: Do you read v1.0.2's commit message directly, or defend your answer?

choices.label: Defend it - the sequence looks fine

auth-recover.speaker: You
auth-recover.narrative: You read it properly. "feat!:" is Conventional Commits' own marker for a breaking change - that should have been v2.0.0, not a PATCH bump.

auth-worse.speaker: Narrator
auth-worse.narrative: You sign off on v1.0.2 as a routine patch. It ships in the combined release notes labeled exactly that way - safe to take without reading further.

auth-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
auth-bad-ending.narrative: Downstream teams upgrade expecting a routine patch, like the version number promised, and every one of them hits the same broken sessions.

ending.debrief: "The sequence looks fine" was never the question - "does this specific commit's own message match its tag" was. v1.0.2's message starts with "feat!:" in plain text. A breaking change wore a patch release's clothes all the way to production because nobody read past the version number.

check-nova-billing.speaker: You
check-nova-billing.narrative: Release 2 of 5: Nova Billing. The previous release, v2.2.0, shipped the initial billing dashboard. The new commit is tagged v2.3.0.
check-nova-billing.prompt: Does v2.3.0's tag match what its own commit says it is?

choices.label: Yes - a "feat:" commit tagged as a MINOR bump is exactly right
No - can't be sure without reading the commit message again

billing-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
billing-flag-note.narrative: You read it again anyway. "feat: add CSV invoice export" - a plain new feature, correctly tagged as a MINOR bump.

check-nova-search.speaker: You
check-nova-search.narrative: Release 3 of 5: Nova Search. The previous release, v4.2.0, was tooling work. The new commit is tagged v4.2.1 - a patch.

s2.message: feat: add fuzzy-search fallback for typo tolerance

check-nova-search.prompt: Does v4.2.1's tag match what its own commit says it is?

choices.label: No - the commit starts with "feat:", a new feature, tagged as a mere patch
Yes - fuzzy-search fallback is a small enough change to count as a patch

search-pushback.speaker: Renata
search-pushback.narrative: "Small enough" isn't a Conventional Commits category, though. What does the commit message itself say this is?"

search-escalate.speaker: You
search-escalate.narrative: You judged the size of the change by feel instead of reading the type marker the commit itself carries.
search-escalate.prompt: Do you read the commit's own type marker, or defend your answer?

choices.label: Read the commit's own type marker
Defend it - fuzzy search is minor enough to be a patch

search-recover.speaker: You
search-recover.narrative: You read it properly. "feat:" - a new feature, whatever its size - belongs in a MINOR bump, not a PATCH one. v4.2.1 should have been v4.3.0.

search-worse.speaker: Narrator
search-worse.narrative: You sign off on v4.2.1 as a routine patch. Teams that only watch for MINOR/MAJOR bumps to know when a new feature landed never see fuzzy search mentioned anywhere in their upgrade notes.

search-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
search-bad-ending.narrative: Months later, a team files a feature request for typo-tolerant search - not realizing it already shipped, buried in what their changelog filter treats as "just patches."

ending.debrief: "Small enough to be a patch" isn't how Conventional Commits works - "feat:" means MINOR, regardless of how modest the change feels. Under-tagging a real feature as a patch doesn't just mislabel a release; it hides the feature from anyone who trusts the version number to tell them what actually shipped.

check-nova-notify.speaker: You
check-nova-notify.narrative: Release 4 of 5: Nova Notify. The previous release, v1.8.0, shipped push notifications. The new commit is tagged v1.9.0.
check-nova-notify.prompt: Does v1.9.0's tag match what its own commit says it is?

choices.label: Yes - a "feat:" commit tagged as a MINOR bump is exactly right
No - can't be sure without reading the commit message again

notify-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
notify-flag-note.narrative: You read it again anyway. "feat: add SMS channel support" - a plain new feature, correctly tagged as a MINOR bump.

check-nova-gateway.speaker: You
check-nova-gateway.narrative: Release 5 of 5: Nova Gateway. The previous release, v5.4.0, was the current baseline. The new commit is tagged v5.4.2 and its message reads "fix: adjust retry backoff timing" - on its face, a fix tagged as a patch, exactly right. But the linked ticket for this change tells a fuller story: the same commit also drops support for the legacy X-Retry-After response header that a few older clients still parse. Nothing about that removal is mentioned in the commit message itself.
check-nova-gateway.prompt: Does v5.4.2's tag correctly reflect what actually shipped?

choices.label: No - dropping a header real clients still depend on is a breaking change, whatever the message calls it
Yes - a "fix:" commit tagged as a patch is exactly right

gateway-pushback.speaker: Renata
gateway-pushback.narrative: "The message says fix, sure - but did you read what the linked ticket says actually changed, or just take the commit's own label at its word?"

gateway-escalate.speaker: You
gateway-escalate.narrative: "The tag matches the message" and "the message matches what actually shipped" stopped being the same claim the moment the commit undersold its own change.
gateway-escalate.prompt: Do you check the ticket for what actually changed, or defend it as compliant?

choices.label: Check the ticket for what actually changed
Defend it - the message says fix, that's what compliant means

gateway-worse.speaker: Narrator
gateway-worse.narrative: You sign off on v5.4.2 as compliant because its message says "fix:" and it's tagged as a patch. Nobody flags that the change quietly drops a response header older clients still rely on.

gateway-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
gateway-bad-ending.narrative: The older clients that parsed X-Retry-After start failing silently, retrying on their own broken schedule. It takes a support escalation from one of them before anyone reads the ticket the commit message never mentioned.

ending.debrief: A commit message that calls itself a "fix:" isn't automatically telling the truth about its own size. Removing something real clients still depend on is a breaking change no matter what label the author chose - and trusting the label instead of what the linked ticket actually describes let it ship as an ordinary patch.

resolution-clean.speaker: Narrator
resolution-clean.narrative: You catch Nova Gateway directly too: its "fix:" message doesn't tell the full story the ticket does. Five releases checked: two under-tagged breaking or feature-sized changes as mere patches (Nova Auth's session change, Nova Search's fuzzy-search fallback), one commit's own message undersold what actually shipped (Nova Gateway), two actually correct (Nova Billing, Nova Notify). You close the release train with the real findings, not a wall of green tags.

good-ending.speaker: Narrator
good-ending.narrative: The combined release notes go out accurate. Nova Auth and Nova Search get recut with the version bumps their commits actually earned, and Nova Gateway's change gets called out as breaking before anyone upgrades expecting a routine patch.

ending.debrief: Three different ways a tag can lie, caught the same way each time: by reading what a commit actually claims to be - in its own type marker, and in the fuller story behind it - instead of trusting how orderly a version sequence looks. That's the whole discipline - Build & Release Management isn't about the numbers going up in order, it's about the number meaning what it says.

check-nova-gateway-b-late.speaker: Narrator
check-nova-gateway-b-late.narrative: You check the ticket directly. It confirms the header removal in plain terms - a breaking change the commit message never mentioned. You flag it.

resolution-recovered.speaker: Narrator
resolution-recovered.narrative: You get to the right call on all five releases in the end. But it took Renata's question to catch that a commit's own label isn't proof of what it actually did.

neutral-ending.speaker: Narrator
neutral-ending.narrative: The release train closes accurate, corrected just before the notes went out.

ending.debrief: You got there - but only because someone else asked whether a "fix:" label is the same as an honest description of what changed. It isn't. Catching that the first time, without needing the question asked back at you, is the habit "which tag lied" ultimately depends on.
